title: The Turncoat at Sekigahara
text:
On 21 October 1600 the two great coalitions of Japan met in a valley at Sekigahara. The Eastern Army was led by Tokugawa Ieyasu. The Western Army was organized by Ishida Mitsunari in the name of the young heir of the late ruler Toyotomi Hideyoshi. On paper the Western side held strong positions on the hills around the valley.

One of those hills, Mount Matsuo, was held by Kobayakawa Hideaki, a young lord with a large force who was related by adoption to the Toyotomi. But Ieyasu had been in secret contact with him for weeks, and Hideaki had agreed to change sides. Ieyasu had made similar arrangements with other Western commanders.

When the battle began in the morning fog, Hideaki did not move. For hours the fighting was hard and indecisive while he watched from his hill. According to a well-known tradition, Ieyasu, angry and impatient, had his troops fire at Mount Matsuo to force a decision. Around midday Hideaki finally came down, not against Ieyasu but against the flank of the Western commander Otani Yoshitsugu. Other Western units then turned as well.

The Western Army collapsed within hours. Ishida Mitsunari was captured and executed. In 1603 Ieyasu became shogun, founding a dynasty that ruled Japan for over 250 years. The battle was won before it began, in the negotiations of the previous weeks.
lesson: Many contests are decided before they start, by the commitments secured in advance. Know who is really on your side, and work on the waverers early.
people: Tokugawa Ieyasu, Kobayakawa Hideaki, Ishida Mitsunari, Otani Yoshitsugu
source: Japanese chronicles of the battle; Anthony J. Bryant, Sekigahara 1600 (1995)
caveat: The story that Ieyasu fired on Kobayakawa's position to force his hand is questioned by some modern historians.
